result.summary: Clark County, Washington, seeks proposals for professional, technical, and expert services as administrator of its Deferred Compensation 457 Plan (RFP #955). Released May 6, 2026, proposals are due June 10, 2026, by 11:00 a.m.; late submissions will not be accepted. Submit one original, two complete copies, and one USB electronic copy by UPS/FedEx or hand delivery to the Clark County Office of Purchasing, 1300 Franklin Street, 6th Floor, Suite 650, Vancouver, WA 98660. USPS and email submissions are unavailable. The office is open weekdays, 8:00 a.m.–3:00 p.m., excluding legal holidays. Questions go to Amie Johnson, Senior Human Resources Representative, at Amie.Johnson@clark.wa.gov or 564-397-2465. Clark County states it is not affiliated with entities not listed on its website and that its emails end in @clark.wa.gov.

result.title: REQUIRED DOCUMENTS:
result.summary: Clark County’s RFP 955 seeks a Deferred Compensation 457 Plan Administrator beginning January 1, 2027. It sets the solicitation schedule, delivery and question procedures, required proposal contents and formatting, eligibility and experience standards, fees and service restrictions, and administrative, legal, disclosure, insurance, accessibility, employment-verification, and other contract obligations. The plan materials cover assets, loans, asset breakdowns, and a questionnaire. Proposals must describe the team, approach, implementation, communications, education, tools, capabilities, and pricing; samples are separate, and responses may become contractual. The section explains plan funding, participants, governance, eligible public-agency use, and contract term and extensions. It details the evaluation’s two scoring tiers, references, and possible finalist interviews. Award procedures include negotiations, implementation requirements, and the County’s authority to reject, revise, waive, postpone, or cancel; public-record access and attached forms are also addressed.

nodes.title: Proposal Requirements
nodes.summary: Clark County seeks a provider for its 457 plan starting January 1, 2027, with goals including stronger participant outcomes, administration, reporting, education, communications, online tools, pricing, and a smooth transition. The section describes the Plan, its participants and assets, Committee authority, funding, eligible public-agency contracting, Title VI protections, proposal deadlines and award schedule, and E-Verify obligations. Respondents must meet experience and asset-size qualifications; avoid specified fees and restrictions; disclose all fund, service, and revenue costs; refrain from promoting unaffiliated products without approval; and satisfy Washington, legal, transition, meeting, and contract requirements. Proposals must follow the ordered questionnaire and submission rules, with samples separated; responses and enhancements may become contractual. The contract covers 2027–2029, with up to seven annual extensions, cost review, and 30-day termination for poor performance. Requirements also cover public works, debarment, ADA accommodations, public-record disclosure and proprietary-marking procedures, insurance, and Plan Holder List registration or Attachment B.

nodes.title: General Information
nodes.summary: Clark County seeks proposals for administration, recordkeeping, education, communications, investment-related and other services for its 457 Deferred Compensation Plan beginning January 1, 2027. Firms not on the Plan Holder List must submit a Letter of Interest; all sections require responses. Under Washington’s Interlocal Cooperation Act, proposers may offer identical services and prices to eligible public agencies, which contract independently. The County has about 1,700 benefit-eligible employees, biweekly Workday payroll, and currently uses Lincoln Financial; plan assets totaled about $167 million on December 31, 2025. Goals include better participant outcomes, competitive plans, integrated administration/reporting, stronger education and communications, online tools, appropriate administrative support, pricing review, lower expenses, orderly transition, and continued Committee-recordkeeper collaboration. The Committee holds fiduciary and administrative authority. Funding depends on the selected proposal. Title VI protections prohibit discrimination and ensure fair bidding opportunity. Timeline: questions May 20, addendum May 22, proposals June 10, finalist meetings July 6–10, decision July 17, notices July 20, negotiations/implementation through December 31, and contract start January 1, 2027. Awardees must register for E-Verify, ensure worker eligibility, and verify compliance; sole proprietors submit a letter.

nodes.title: Work Requirements
nodes.summary: The County requires RFP respondents to certify they meet or agree to the minimum qualifications: at least five years administering governmental Section 457 plans and sole administration of at least three plans, each with $100 million or more in assets. Contracts must have no front- or back-end charges or transfer/withdrawal restrictions or penalties, except specified capital-preservation equity-wash/put provisions and mutual-fund short-term trading fees. Firms must fully disclose fund and service expenses and revenue, including for fixed/general accounts and services such as managed accounts, advice, planning, and brokerage. They may not sell or promote unaffiliated products without written Committee approval. The awarded firm must be qualified to do business in Washington, transition existing loans, attend Committee meetings as required, and comply with applicable County, state, and federal laws and contract rules. RFP response terms and enhancements must remain in force through negotiations and enter the final contract unless waived in writing; submitting a response implies compliance unless adjusted or waived by written addendum.

nodes.title: REQUIRED DOCUMENTS:
nodes.summary: Proposals must follow the ordered Exhibit C questionnaire, formatting, page and word limits, answer-box rules, and attachment instructions; requested samples belong in a separate electronic folder. Submitted materials and enhancements may become contractual. The County will assist with implementation and communications. The contract runs 2027–2029, with up to seven annual extensions, cost review, and termination on 30 days’ notice for unsatisfactory performance. Public-work requirements, debarment certification, ADA accommodations, and public-record disclosure rules apply; proprietary material must be marked, and a court order sought within 10 days to prevent release. Insurance requirements include workers’ compensation; auto, general, professional, umbrella, fiduciary, and employee-dishonesty coverage; specified limits, deductibles, endorsements, additional-insured status, subrogation waivers, proof, and cancellation notice. Proposers must be on the Plan Holders List or submit Attachment B; unlisted proposals may be nonresponsive.

nodes.title: REQUIRED DOCUMENTS: (intro)
nodes.summary: Proposals must include an ordered Exhibit C questionnaire in 10-point Calibri, within 50 pages excluding cover letter/exhibits, following word limits and answer-box rules, and no unrequested attachments; requested samples/descriptions go in a separate electronic exhibit folder. Submitted materials and later enhancements may form part of the contract. County benefits/payroll staff will support implementation and employee communications; schedule refers to the selection timeline, and place of performance is not applicable. The contract runs Jan. 1, 2027–Dec. 31, 2029, with up to seven annual extensions (cost reviewed) and termination on 30 days’ notice for unsatisfactory performance. Public-work prevailing-wage, filing, and fee requirements apply. Debarred/suspended suppliers are ineligible; a signed certification is required. ADA accommodations are available. Submittals are public records; mark protected portions “PROPRIETARY,” and seek a court order within 10 days of notice to prevent release. Insurance terms require subrogation waivers, proof and cancellation notice, workers’ compensation, specified auto and general-liability coverage, and professional-liability insurance.

nodes.title: RFP Disclosure and Insurance Requirements
nodes.summary: Respondents have 10 days to obtain a court order preventing disclosure of records; otherwise, the County may release records subject to disclosure and is not liable for resulting losses. Insurance must waive subrogation against the County and related personnel, with equivalent waivers required from subcontractors. Before work begins, provide ACORD certificates showing coverage, deductibles, and policy periods; policies must provide 30 days’ mailed notice of cancellation or reduction, and the proposer must document continued coverage during overlap periods. Washington workers’ compensation laws apply. If vehicles are used, commercial auto coverage must include owned and non-owned vehicles, with $1 million per occurrence and annual aggregate limits; otherwise, submit written confirmation. CGL must provide specified occurrence, aggregate, and personal/advertising injury limits, renew annually, allow qualifying primary/umbrella/excess coverage, and maintain products/completed-operations coverage for three years after substantial completion. Deductibles are capped at $50,000 absent County approval; specified coverage exclusions are prohibited, and Clark County must be an additional insured.

nodes.title: F. Professional Liability (aka Errors and Omissions)
nodes.summary:
F. Professional Liability (aka Errors and Omissions)
The Proposer shall obtain, at Proposers expense, and keep in force during the term of this contract Professional Liability insurance policy to protect against legal liability arising out ofRequest for Proposal #955 Deferred Compensation 457 Plan Administrator
contract activity. Such insurance shall provide a minimum of $1,000,000 per occurrence. The deductible will not be more than $25,000 unless prior arrangements are made with Clark County on a case-by-case basis; the criterion is the Proposers liquidity and ability to pay from its own resources. It should be an “Occurrence Form” policy. If the policy is “Claims Made”, then Extended Reporting Period Coverage (Tail coverage) shall be purchased for three (3) years after the end of the contract.

nodes.title: G. Umbrella Liability Coverage
nodes.summary:
G. Umbrella Liability Coverage
Umbrella Coverage in the amount of $1,000,000 shall be provided and will apply over all liability policies without exception, including Commercial General Liability and Automobile Liability.

nodes.title: H. Additional Insured
key_items: I. Fiduciary Liability in the amount of $1,000,000 per occurrence and $3,000,000 annual aggregate.
nodes.summary: Contractors and subcontractors must name Clark County and its officers, employees, and agents as additional insureds on all policies, including unrestricted products and completed-operations coverage; coverage must be primary and noncontributory. The contractor must provide proof and required endorsements, and certified policy copies upon request. Insurers must be authorized in Washington and rated at least A-VII by Best’s. Required limits include fiduciary liability of $1 million per occurrence and $3 million aggregate, plus employee dishonesty coverage of at least $1 million. All proposers must appear on the Plan Holders List, verify their listing before submitting, and submit Attachment B, a Letter of Interest, if absent; proposals from unlisted proposers may be deemed nonresponsive. The list is available on Clark County’s RFP website.

nodes.title: Part II Proposal Preparation and Submittal
nodes.summary: No pre-submittal meeting is planned. Questions about the RFP must be emailed to the contact on the cover by May 20, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. Pacific; substantive clarifications will be issued by addendum by May 22. Proposers should review the Q&A at the Clark County RFP site. Sealed proposals are due at the date, time, and location on the cover; packages must show the RFP number and title, and proposer name and address. Late proposals are returned unopened; insufficient copies may be rejected. Proposals must be clear, complete, and no more than 50 pages, excluding resumes, cover sheet, and debarment form; excess pages may not be reviewed. Recyclable, recycled-content materials and double-sided printing are encouraged; color is acceptable, and extra brochures should be omitted unless requested. Required content includes Attachment A cover sheet; project-team structure; management approach, implementation timeline, communications and education/enrollment tools, and Exhibit C questionnaire; respondent capabilities; project approach and understanding; and applicable fees in Exhibit C.

nodes.title: Part III Proposal Evaluation & Contract Award
nodes.summary: The County Committee will review all properly submitted proposals and select a firm using the RFP and questionnaire criteria, references, and possibly interviews. Interviews may be required for shortlisted firms, will be virtual, and are tentatively scheduled for July 2026; references will be checked for all proposers. Proposals will be objectively scored in two tiers, each worth 100 points (200 total). Tier 1—initial review: proposal approach/quality (10), employee support and experience (20), administrative support (20), financial (25), fund lineup (15), and performance guarantees (10). Tier 2—finalist presentations/best and final offers: finalist presentation (25), employee/employer portal capabilities (30), final cost (30), and references (15).

nodes.title: Contract Award
nodes.summary: Clark County will select the most qualified proposer using weighted criteria, proposer attributes, and proposal responsiveness. If negotiations fail with the top proposer, the County will approach the next qualified proposer; if no agreement is reached, it may void the RFP. The County may accept or reject proposals, negotiate changes, waive formalities, postpone or cancel the award, and award based on its best interests. The successful proposer’s proposal and responses may become part of the contract. RFP documents are available to the public through a public records request. Vendors must provide an implementation plan in their proposal or finalist interview, and the carrier must lead implementation and ensure activities finish before the effective date.

result.title: Certification Regarding
result.summary: This section contains a prospective-participant certification concerning debarment, exclusions, relevant convictions or judgments, pending charges, and public-transaction terminations, with consequences for false statements and fields for an authorized signature or an explanation if unable to certify. Exhibits report Clark County and CRESA retirement-plan assets and activity, including contributions, distributions, hardship requests, loans, education, fixed-income terms, and managed-account and brokerage provisions. Investment menus list fund options, assets, fees, revenue sharing, redemption terms, and addition dates. The section also sets questionnaire response rules, page limits, exhibits, and an 11-tab submission structure covering provider background and qualifications; plan, recordkeeping, technology, security, custody, participant and sponsor services; investments, fees, liquidity, guarantees, and transition planning; pricing, performance, penalties, revenue sharing, disclosures, administration, reporting, and governmental-client references.

nodes.title: Clark County, Washington
key_items: Certification Regarding Debarment, Suspension and Other Responsibility Matters
nodes.summary: The prospective participant certifies that it and its principals are not currently debarred, suspended, proposed for debarment, ineligible, or voluntarily excluded from covered public transactions; have not, in the preceding three years, had relevant fraud, criminal, antitrust, or other listed convictions or civil judgments; are not currently charged with those offenses; and have not had a public transaction terminated for cause or default during that period. A false statement may lead to proposal rejection or award termination and, under 18 U.S.C. § 1001, a fine of up to $10,000, imprisonment for up to five years, or both. The form provides fields for company name, authorized representative’s typed name and title, signature, and date, and allows an applicant unable to certify to attach an explanation.

nodes.title: EXHIBIT A
nodes.summary: Exhibit A reports retirement-plan assets and activity for Clark County (CCWA-001) and participating employer CRESA (CCWA-002), including accounts, deferrals, roll-ins, contributions, distributions, net cash flow and hardship requests/approvals. County assets rose from $111.5 million in 2022 to $162.8 million in 2025; CRESA held $5.06 million in 2025. Both plans share an investment lineup and fees, and no participants used Morningstar managed accounts at year-end 2025. The County offers no self-directed brokerage option; the exhibit also includes unlabeled annual financial and count data for 2022–2024. Managed accounts are not currently offered, though bid scenarios may include them subject to utilization/fee reporting, performance reporting on request, County termination rights without a recordkeeping-fee change, and no fee increases. Fixed-income rates, guarantees, floor and termination options are reported, along with loan balances, counts and defaults, and 2024–2025 education activity. Exhibit B lists Lincoln Financial’s investment menu, fees, revenue shares, assets, redemption terms and addition dates; revenue shares are zero and total assets are $161,956,444.

nodes.title: MANAGED ACCOUNT SERVICE:

MANAGED ACCOUNT SERVICE:
Managed account services are not currently offered. The County is not interested in adding this feature currently. However, the Plan Sponsor regularly evaluates plan features and thus, bid scenarios with Managed Accounts and without may be submitted. Please note that any Managed Account bid scenario also includes the following minimum requirements:
• Respondents will regularly report (at least semi-annually) Managed Account age demographic utilization and clearly report all fees paid by participants for the service.
• Managed Account reporting will include performance metrics when requested.• Respondents also agree that the Managed Account service may be turned off by the County at any time and the proposed Recordkeeping fee will remain for the contract duration.
• Managed Account fees will not increase during the contract.

nodes.title: RESPONDING TO THE QUESTIONNAIRE
nodes.summary: Sets response-format rules, page limits, required exhibits and the 11-tab submission structure. Requests firm background, ownership, revenues, insurance, financial condition, litigation, regulation, staffing, public-sector experience, plan and asset data, wins/losses, and affiliations. Covers recordkeeping systems, audits, payroll, contributions, account features, cybersecurity, fraud protection, custody and insurance. Assesses participant advice, education, communications, statements, digital and transaction services, call centers, and plan-sponsor support, reporting, outsourcing, compliance and legal services. Seeks investment and capital-preservation details, fees, liquidity, guarantees, annuities, and self-directed brokerage options. Requires transition plans, experience, staffing, education, blackout and asset-transfer information. Requests service and investment pricing across contract terms, transaction and other fees, and performance benchmarks, financial penalties, reporting and guarantee-payment history. Addresses revenue-sharing rebates, sponsor fee collection and administration, disclosures, account handling and reporting, and references from current, former and transition governmental 457 clients.

nodes.title: EXHIBIT C
nodes.summary: Responses should be clear and concise. Yes/No questions need explanations only when requested; requested explanations should focus on the main relevant points. Reproduce each question before its answer, complete required tables (using a replicated table no larger than the sample), and separate answers to multiple questions. Provide requested descriptions or samples in a separate Proposing Firm Exhibit Folder, and include no unrequested exhibits. The response is organized into 11 tabs: Tab 1, cover letter (2-page limit); Tab 2, RFP response for Sections A–G (50-page limit); and Tabs 3–11, Exhibits 1–9: insurance rating agency report, SOC 1 audit reports, control objective results, sample quarterly participant statement, fee disclosure sample, capital preservation fund fact sheet, list of proprietary and alliance funds, sample participant brokerage statement, and sample transition plan.

nodes.title: A. FIRM STRENGTH, EXPERIENCE AND QUALIFICATIONS
nodes.summary: The section requests the firm’s RFP contact, founding year and 457 public-sector experience, ownership and organizational details, subsidiaries, and 2022–2025 company and retirement-services revenue. It covers insurance policies, limits, deductibles and underwriters; ownership or transaction discussions and changes; bankruptcy or insolvency; financial-covenant breaches; credit ratings and agency reports; financial ratios and results; litigation, investigations and other matters affecting performance; regulatory citations or penalties; and employee counts. For firms working on defined-contribution plans or solely serving public-sector plans, it requests 2021–2025 asset, product, managed-account and governmental-plan usage data; public-sector 457 plan assets, participants and provider counts by plan size; plans won and lost by asset band, including decisions not to rebid; and details of organizational or industry-group affiliations or endorsements, including relationships, payments, contributions and duration.

nodes.title: Firm was founded: 457 public sector plans:
nodes.summary: A firm-strength, experience, and qualifications questionnaire requesting: a single RFP contact’s name, title, address, phone, and email; the firm’s founding year and when it began administering 457 public-sector plans; business details including public/private status, parent location and name, structure, and number of subsidiaries; total company and retirement-plan-services revenue for 2025–2022; applicable insurance policy types (errors and omissions, directors and officers, general liability, financial institution bond, cybersecurity, workers’ compensation, and auto), with limits, deductibles, and underwriters; whether purchase, merger, sale, or ownership-change discussions, agreements, or changes occurred, including changes in the past five years, with yes/no, year, and brief descriptions; and whether the organization has ever filed for bankruptcy or become insolvent, with yes/no and date.

nodes.title: Bankruptcy Insolvent
nodes.summary: The section covers bankruptcy/insolvency; whether the organization has breached financial covenants, with dates and liabilities; organizational or parent-company credit ratings (including insurers’ financial-strength and counterparty ratings, rating dates, and the latest agency report as Exhibit 1); and revenue, net income, current ratio, quick ratio, and debt-to-equity ratio for 2025 and 2024. It asks about litigation and other potentially adverse matters affecting RFP performance, including case details, status, amounts, investigations, and brief descriptions. It also asks whether the organization, parent, local representatives, or proposed subcontractors faced regulatory citations or penalties in the past ten years, with names, years, agencies, and violations, and requests the total number of employees represented.

nodes.title: Firm employees: Working on DC plans: Solely serving public sector plans:
nodes.summary: The text requests information for firms working on defined contribution (DC) plans and those solely serving public-sector plans. Tables cover 2021–2025 DC plan assets in proprietary and non-proprietary products, managed-account assets, and governmental plan and participant usage rates. It asks for 2021–2025 public-sector recordkept 457 plan assets and participant counts, plus 2025 plan counts, assets, and sole-provider counts by participant-size and asset-size bands. It also requests public-sector DC plans won and lost by asset-size band for 2020–2025, including decisions not to rebid but excluding retentions without meaningful asset growth. Finally, it asks whether the organization has affiliations or endorsements from organizations or industry groups and, if so, their relationships, monetary status, contribution amounts, and duration.

nodes.title: B. RECORD KEEPING, CYBER SECURITY AND CUSTODY
nodes.summary: The section covers recordkeeping-system ownership, launch date, participant and plan counts, infrastructure, SOC 1/2 reports, control-audit findings, and sponsor audit rights. It addresses payroll and loan-deduction file formats and transfer methods, contribution and funding deadlines, participant error-reporting periods, and responsibility and limits for correcting errors. It also covers tiered investment menus; Roth deferrals and in-service conversions; separate traditional/Roth allocations and account reporting; percentage or dollar deferrals; and paperless enrollment and statements, including default options. Cybersecurity topics include access controls for current and archived participant data, AI use, backup practices and locations, COVID-related changes, encryption, breaches, data-sharing vendors, and audit schedules and findings. Account protections include multifactor and non-SSN logins, password standards, breach monitoring, and reimbursement for cyber or fraud losses. Custody topics include trustee/custodian identity and tenure, insurance coverage and terms, underwriters, and model trust agreements.

nodes.title: RECORD KEEPING:
nodes.summary: A recordkeeping, cybersecurity, and custody questionnaire asks about the system’s proprietary status, start date, participant and plan counts, and server/mainframe basis; requires SOC 1 and SOC 2 reports and recent audit control results, including exceptions; and asks whether authorized Plan Sponsor representatives may conduct audits. It covers payroll contribution and loan-deduction file formats and transfer protocols, daily contribution-file/funding deadlines, participant error-reporting windows, and responsibility for making participants or plans whole for controlled errors, including dollar and time limits. It asks whether investment menus can be tiered on paper and online/mobile; whether the firm offers Roth 457 deferrals and in-service conversions; whether traditional and Roth contributions can have separate allocations, and how self-directed accounts and statements handle both tax types. It also asks whether deferrals can be specified as percentages or dollar amounts, whether enrollment and statements can be paperless and what each requires, and whether paperless statements may be the default.

nodes.title: CYBER SECURITY/AI:
nodes.summary: Covers data-security procedures and control/monitoring of access to current and archived participant data, including viewing, printing, and removing it; use of AI and its impact on participant data; backup frequency, COVID-related changes, offsite locations, and encryption at rest and in transit. It asks about security breaches, external vendors or partners receiving participant information and what is shared, and audit frequency, most recent audit, auditor, and findings. Account safeguards include multifactor and unique non-SSN logins, password requirements, breach-monitoring services and vendors, and reimbursement policies and limits for cyber or fraud losses. Custody topics include the trustee/custodian and relationship length, its insurance types, limits, deductibles, and underwriters, and whether the firm offers a model trust agreement.

nodes.title: C. PARTICIPANT SERVICES
nodes.summary: The section evaluates participant services, including online advice and managed accounts: providers, launch dates, public-sector client and plan counts, assets, utilization, sponsor flexibility, investment-option sources for distributions, fiduciary responsibility, and contracting requirements. It covers communication and education staffing, qualifications, licensing, training, disclosures, availability, response times, meeting commitments, sponsor resources, assignment and complaint processes, compensation and incentives, financial planning, behavior and campaign measurement, quarterly reporting, collaboration, retirement-readiness tools, surveys and costs, customized materials, and webinars. It also assesses statements and technology: statement content, aggregation, delivery, online availability, retention and samples; services and transactions across phone, desktop, voice response and mobile; paper options, loans and transfer cutoffs; test access and password procedures; distribution processing and payment, fund and tax choices; and service-center locations, hours, staffing and licenses. Call-center and website performance statistics, including response times, call duration, dropped calls, channel usage and staff turnover from 2022–2025, are requested.

nodes.title: ON-LINE ADVICE / MANAGED ACCOUNT SERVICES:
nodes.summary: The section asks whether the firm offers online advice and/or managed account services to plan participants. If so, it requests each service provider and service name, start date, public-sector participant and plan counts, assets, and average participant utilization per plan. It also asks whether the sponsor may offer online advice without managed accounts, whether managed-account distributions can come from a specific investment option such as Stable Value, whether the firm or its advice partner assumes fiduciary responsibility, and whether the sponsor must contract separately with a partner providing investment advice.

nodes.title: COMMUNICATION AND EDUCATION:
nodes.summary: The section asks providers to describe participant-service staffing, including representatives’ experience, caseloads, credentials, schedules, response times, required licenses and training, and FINRA Form U-4 disclosure events. It covers online investment advice and comprehensive financial planning, provider qualifications, annual meeting hours and days, and resources required from the Plan Sponsor. Providers must explain representative work locations, sponsor input on assignments, handling dissatisfaction, individual and group meetings, and proposed annual on-site service commitments. Compensation, employment status, bonuses, and product- or service-related sales incentives for staff are requested. The section also asks how providers measure participant behavior and campaign effectiveness, report results quarterly, and collaborate with sponsors on communication strategies; whether they offer retirement-readiness or income-gap tools across statements, websites, and mobile devices; and whether they conduct surveys, including frequency and costs. Finally, it asks about customized educational materials across communication channels and education delivered through webinars, including interactive webinars.

nodes.title: Participant Service Staffing and Qualifications
key_items: FINRA Series 7 FINRA Series 63 FINRA Series 65
nodes.summary: The page asks how many on-site representatives are proposed to serve the plan sponsor and requests details for two representatives, including name, tenure, location, client accounts, assets and participants served, education, credentials and licenses, work schedule, and response-time commitments. It also asks which certifications, licenses, and training are required for participant investment-advice providers, distinguishing on-site from call-center staff and indicating whether FINRA Series 7, 63, and 65, CFP, CFA, or other qualifications apply. Finally, it asks which FINRA or insurance licenses on-site representatives must hold.

nodes.title: Required FINRA Series Required Insurance Licenses
nodes.summary: The text requests information on required FINRA Series and insurance licenses, and asks whether procurement-assigned individuals have FINRA Form U-4s or disclosure events (C10). It asks whether the firm will provide online investment advice with help from on-site representatives, who may explain the tool, enter data, and review its results with participants; respondents must state annual meetings, total hours, and whether those hours include or exclude proposed education hours (C11). It asks whether comprehensive financial planning will be offered (C12), whether it will be provided through a Certified Financial Planner (C13), and whether planners have FINRA U-4s or disclosure events (C14). For proposed financial-planning service days, it requests annual meeting count, total hours, and how those hours relate to education hours (C15). Finally, it asks what physical and personnel resources the firm will provide or require from the Plan Sponsor for on-site services (C16).

nodes.title: Onsite resources: (100 word limit)
nodes.summary: The section asks whether participant service representatives will work from home, an office, or both; whether the Plan Sponsor can help select assigned representatives; how the firm would address dissatisfaction with assigned personnel; and whether it will provide on-site individual meetings and group sessions at sponsor-specified locations and times. It also requests a proposed annual on-site enrollment and education commitment, based on sponsor demographics and firm experience, stated as total contract hours and days. Partial service days must be counted proportionally, not as full days. Response limits are specified for some questions.

nodes.title: Proposed annual number of on-site service hours: Proposed annual number of on-site service days:

C22 requests compensation details for employees, certified financial planners, and contractors who meet face-to-face with participants, including account, phone, education, and investment-advice representatives; bonus criteria (up to 50 words); employment status (W-2 or 1099); fixed and bonus compensation percentages; and whether compensation is one-time, recurring, or investment/product-dependent. C23 asks whether on-site representatives, plan sponsor representatives, or other employees receive incentives to sell specified services or products, with yes/no responses and tables by role. These include online advice, managed accounts, guaranteed minimum withdrawal benefits, IRA rollovers, managed payout options, fixed/general account or stable value, proprietary mutual funds, Roth/traditional/rollover IRAs, and other products. C24 asks how the organization measures or benchmarks the effects of communication and education on participant behavior, limited to 200 words.

nodes.title: STATEMENTS/SYSTEM TECHNOLOGY:
nodes.summary: Covers statement capabilities and content, including account aggregation and persistence, defined-benefit information, sponsor messaging, investment performance, balances, contributions, cash flows, loans, returns, fees, asset allocation, and retirement projections/readiness. Requests statement delivery and online timing, retention, samples, and on-demand periods; compares participant services and actions across phone, voice response, desktop, and mobile, including outside vendors, paper options, online loans, and transfer cutoffs. Requests test website/mobile access credentials and password assignment/change procedures; distribution processing times and participant choices for payment dates, fund sources, ordering, and tax sources. Also asks service-center locations, operating hours, staffing, representative securities licenses, and call-center/website statistics—including response and call duration, dropped calls, channel transaction shares, and staff turnover—for 2022–2025.

nodes.title: Explanation: (100 word limit)
nodes.summary: The questionnaire asks whether statements aggregate multiple accounts; which outside accounts can be aggregated and whether their details persist across log-ins; whether defined-benefit information can appear in statements or retirement analyses; and whether sponsors can customize statement messages. It requests yes/no availability of statement details: fund performance (monthly, quarterly, and 1-, 3-, 5- and 10-year), quarterly cash flow and Roth deferrals, asset allocation, total and Roth assets, loans and repayments, personal rate of return, expense ratios, defined-benefit assets, projected retirement income, and readiness score. It asks statement delivery/online availability timing, retention period, a sample statement, and on-demand statements for selected periods. A channel-by-channel (phone representatives, voice response, desktop, mobile) table covers balances, investments, contributions, transactions, loans, beneficiaries, performance/advice, online actions and applications, distributions, retirement projections, and mobile features. It also asks about outside vendors, paper enrollment/account changes, sponsor website messages, online loan applications and end-to-end completion, and the daily transfer-request cutoff time in the sponsor’s time zone.

nodes.title: D. PLAN SPONSOR SERVICES
nodes.summary: A Plan Sponsor services questionnaire covering: day-to-day relationship and account managers’ qualifications, workload, availability, response times, meeting attendance, sponsor participation in selection, and handling dissatisfaction; client satisfaction survey frequency and responsibility; sponsor-staff online/paper capabilities and effective dates for participant-account tasks; available reports, delivery frequency and formats, and access to raw data/customizable reporting; demo website credentials; administrative functions eligible for full outsourcing; online sponsor services and loan-default notifications and assistance; participant loan applications, repayment options after separation, ACH administration, and payroll deduction transmission; public-sector plan automatic-enrollment and Roth-deferral statistics by year; contribution-type identification requirements; additional outsourcing services; communications and education compliance, Section 404(c), fee disclosures, and indemnification; legal and tax-code compliance support and regulatory-change notices; maintenance and cost of model plan documents; and sponsor newsletters.

nodes.title: E. INVESTMENT FLEXIBILITY
nodes.summary: Covers capital-preservation products, including proprietary-product requirements, crediting formulas and rates, 10-year quarterly returns, GIPS compliance and audits, annual market-to-book ratios and crediting rates, Exhibit 6 attribution, wrap-provider capacity, ratings, allocations and fees, liquidity provisions, termination treatment and market-value adjustments. Requests investment benchmarks; non-revenue-sharing products, costs and rates; floor rates and contract terms; put-period notice, trading limits, redemption fees and notifications, processing times and fund-change schedules. Also addresses restrictions on adding funds, compensation outside revenue sharing, non-NSCC options and fees, and an Exhibit 7 investment-option list. Covers recordkeeping and fees for trusts, general accounts, separate accounts and annuity/guaranteed-income products; GMWB costs, portability, TPA support and SECURE Act IRA transfers. For SDBAs, asks about availability, brokerage provider, tradable/restricted assets, asset limits, core-balance minimums, transfers, timing restrictions, direct deferrals, Roth and tax-source handling, quarterly statements, and a sample participant statement for Exhibit 8.

nodes.title: Required Proprietary Product Name
nodes.summary: The section requests information on capital-preservation investment options: whether enhanced pricing requires a proprietary product and its name; the crediting-rate formula and current rate; quarterly net returns for the past 10 years; whether returns are GIPS-compliant and audited; and annual market-to-book ratios (or equivalent) and net annualized crediting rates for 2014–2025. It also requires a recent sector and wrap-provider attribution sheet labeled Exhibit 6, plus proprietary-product wrap-provider details, including additional capacity, S&P rating, portfolio share, and fee. Respondents must describe participant and plan-sponsor liquidity provisions (each within 50 words), explain termination liquidity by product type (book- or market-value liquidation, put period, and in-kind securities), and provide any market-value adjustment formula applicable to enhanced-pricing products.

nodes.title: Formula: (100 word limit)
nodes.summary: The questionnaire asks for the benchmark used to assess proposed capital-preservation investments (with a 100-word response limit); available non-revenue-sharing stable-value/capital-preservation products, including expense ratio, current net credit rate, and proprietary status; and proposed stable-value or fixed-option floor rates and contract terms. It also asks whether sponsors may give advance notice to start a put period and later keep the fund without charges; whether participant trading-frequency limits apply; whether short-term trading restrictions and redemption fees can be imposed and are applied according to fund-company policies; whether participants are notified of applicable redemption fees; and how many days fund additions or removals take after instructions.

nodes.title: Number of days:
nodes.summary: The questionnaire asks whether fund additions and deletions follow a monthly, quarterly, or annual schedule; what restrictions apply to adding funds; whether the firm receives compensation from fund companies outside revenue-sharing agreements and how many companies pay it; and whether non-NSCC-eligible options are processed and at what additional fee. It requests an asset-class-segmented Excel list of proprietary and alliance investment options, including tickers, expense ratios, and available revenue-share information, labeled Exhibit 7. Respondents must indicate recordkeeping availability and fees for non-proprietary commingled trusts, general accounts, separate accounts, and annuity or guaranteed-retirement-income products. It also asks whether the firm offers a guaranteed minimum withdrawal benefit (GMWB), with product name, investment and insurance costs, and portability to another recordkeeper; if so, whether third-party administrators may record-keep it and which TPA firms currently provide it to defined-contribution plans.

nodes.title: Fund Compensation, Investment Options, and Recordkeeping
nodes.summary: The page asks whether the firm receives compensation from fund companies outside revenue-sharing agreements and how many companies pay it; whether it processes non-NSCC-eligible options and charges fees; and whether it can provide an asset-class-segmented Excel list of proprietary and alliance investment options, including ticker symbols, expense ratios, and revenue-sharing information, for Exhibit 7. It also asks about recordkeeping availability and fees for non-proprietary commingled trusts, general accounts, separate accounts, and annuity or guaranteed-income products. Finally, it covers whether the firm offers a guaranteed minimum withdrawal benefit (GMWB), its product name, investment and insurance costs, portability, and whether third-party administrators can record-keep it, including the names of current TPA providers.

nodes.title: F. TRANSITION
key_items: Blackout on your system: Total blackout days:
nodes.summary: Requests a one-page transition plan for a January 1, 2027 contract start (Exhibit 9); counts of plans transitioned from other providers by asset-size tier for 2020–2025 and total; minimum and typical transition durations; whether the implementation timeframe is guaranteed; and whether a dedicated transition team will be provided, including members, roles, and prior transitions from the current recordkeeper. It also asks for proposed transition-period onsite education hours and days, and whether these supplement Section C commitments, counting partial days proportionally. The provider must describe its handling of systematic distributions, communications to retired or separated employees, emergency requests during blackout, and prohibited transactions. It asks for anticipated system and total blackout days, time assets are out of the market, and whether in-kind assets/shares and self-directed brokerage assets can be transferred.

nodes.title: G. Fees and Expenses Proposal
nodes.summary: The section requests proposed annual recordkeeping, administration, participant and plan-sponsor services, and on-site education/counseling fees, both per participant and as a percentage of assets, with and without proprietary products. Pricing is requested for 5-, 7-, and 10-year terms, including whether extended terms are offered without guarantee; longer-term pricing assumes contract renewal. Respondents must describe termination rights and notice, identify products exempt from revenue requirements, and provide self-directed brokerage setup, maintenance, trading fees, revenue, revenue-crediting, and administrative-fee details. It also requests financial-planning, investment-advice, online-advice, and managed-account fees and whether fees apply to all participants or users and count toward pricing requirements. Fee schedules are requested for participant administration (loans, withdrawals, distributions, QDROs, and related transactions), plan-sponsor administration (reporting, documents, compliance, searches, audits, communications, and fund changes), and any other non-asset-based services.

nodes.title: PERFORMANCE GUARANTEES
nodes.summary: The section asks respondents to specify performance benchmarks and dollars at risk for failing them, across phone response and call returns; participant and sponsor statement mailing and online posting; on-site individual and group meetings, financial planning, participation and deferral increases; transition timelines, deliverables and meetings; administration of contributions, withdrawals, emergency withdrawals, rollovers/transfers and loans; report delivery and training; and survey distribution and satisfaction scores. It also asks whether service-performance reports will be provided to the plan sponsor and how frequently, and whether the provider has paid clients for failing such guarantees, including the number of payments in the past three years.

nodes.title: FEE ADMINISTRATION
key_items: Current Governmental Client References; Former/Terminated Client References; Transition References
nodes.summary: The fee-administration questions ask whether excess investment revenue sharing will be rebated and how often; whether the firm will collect and return sponsor-imposed asset-based administration fees, including calculation and frequency; account setup and investment choices for fee assets, whether the investment must be on the core menu, and whether/how the firm holds and provides access to those assets. They also ask about quarterly statements, transaction cash-flow labels and dates, hard-dollar annual participant fee caps, written disclosure of all investment and service revenues, and monthly or at least quarterly admin-account reports with transaction descriptions. Reference requests cover two current governmental 457 clients with at least $100 million in assets, two former clients served within five years, and two governmental 457 transition clients with approximately $100 million in assets transitioned within three years. For each, provide client and contact details, plan inception date, and total assets; transition contacts should have been directly involved, and one current client should preferably be a California agency.
